text: Thornfield Materials Holdings, ticket forty-six-twelve. The controller is trying to close October for the Fixtures Division ledger and it won't close — no idea which subsidiary is the problem. Critical severity, this blocks the consolidated close.

Quick context on period status: Never Opened means no transactions at all. Future Enterable allows journal entry but not posting. Open allows full activity. Closed blocks new transactions but can potentially reopen. Permanently Closed has no path back. And closing a period isn't one action — it's a checklist: every subledger transferred and accounted, every GL journal posted, reconciliations complete where required.

Opening the Close Monitor for this ledger and period shows exactly what's unmet, instead of one opaque can't-close message. Two items: six Receivables journals for October still unposted, and one Payables batch accounted Final but never transferred to GL. Here's the thing worth noticing — neither of these is new. The six unposted journals look exactly like lesson sixteen's ticket. The untransferred Payables batch looks exactly like lesson eight or lesson nineteen.

So you work each one the way you already know how. The six journals: one references a disabled account, same pattern as before — corrected and posted. The Payables batch: confirmed a genuine timing gap, not an intentional exclusion — Transfer to GL run manually, then posted. Once the Close Monitor shows every prerequisite met, the period actually closes.

A stuck period close is almost never a new category of problem — it's one or more tickets you already know how to work, just surfaced by the close checklist instead of an individual complaint. That's why this lesson comes last in the chapter. Up next, chapter five: Assets, Expenses, and Setup tickets, starting with depreciation that didn't run.
